items.title: Tifereth Israel Honors the Pikelnys
items.caption: Congregation Tifereth Israel honored Rabbi Dov B. Pikelny and Barbara D. Pikelny for 13 years of service.
items.description: October 1994 recognition of Rabbi Dov B. Pikelny and Cantor Barbara Pikelny for 13 years of service.
items.source: The Journal, October 21, 1994, page 38
items.citation: The Journal, October 21, 1994, p. 38
items.transcript:
Congregation Tifereth Israel, the Sephardic shul of Peabody, celebrated the thirteenth year of involvement of Rabbi Dov B. and Barbara Pikelny. The region’s only Sephardic synagogue at 8 Pierpont Street expressed its appreciation for their contributions to the synagogue and the congregation.

The social hall was the setting for an overflow crowd of 150 who showed their appreciation to the rabbi and rebbetzin. “It’s a family style congregation,” said Rabbi Pikelny. “The founders of the shul all came from Turkey. They were related or their families married here.”

Barbara Pikelny had been “the only female cantor in the North Shore,” according to Rabbi Pikelny, “until she suffered a stroke several years ago. She never fully recovered, and is now a resident of the Abbott House Nursing Home of Lynn where she is pleased to receive visitors,” he added.

Barbara Pikelny was a great influence in the synagogue until she took ill, said the rabbi. The theme of the event, with the 13 candles for each year that the couple has been involved, also symbolized the areas in which Barbara had an impact on the congregation, said Pikelny.

items.title: Our First Religious Leaders: Joseph Havien, David Leon, and Ralph Bencangey
items.caption: Historical tribute to Joseph Havien, David Leon, and Ralph Bencangey, who led early Sephardic worship in the Peabody–Salem area.
items.description: Historical page honoring Joseph Havien, David Leon, and Ralph Bencangey as the congregation's early religious and spiritual leaders. The text says they arrived in the United States in 1914, held services in homes, and later established a dedicated room for worship. Publication date not established.
items.source: CTI historical commemorative page, supplied by user; publication date unknown
items.transcript:
OUR RELIGIOUS LEADERS

Mr. Joseph Havien, Mr. David Leon and Mr. Ralph Bencangey, our three religious and spiritual leaders, came to these United States in 1914 and settled in Peabody-Salem area. Assisted by only a very small group of families of the Spanish Jewish faith, they, with their wealth of Jewish culture and inspiration, conducted services in each other's homes. In later years, when the Sephardic community became larger, they hired a room and with everyone taking part, transformed it into a place of worship. In the small, but highly significant Synagogue, the three above mentioned men conducted all the services. These men always have given their all for the perpetuation of the Jewish religion and for the law of God. Repeatedly they have told us: "Be sincere, faithful, tolerant, a good Jew, and make America strong."

items.transcript:
October 3, 1972

PEABODY — In 1911, a small band of Jews came to this area from Turkey.

These people, who traced their lineage back to pre-Christian Spain, formed the original congregation of Tifereth Israel, on Pierpont St., which celebrates its 50th anniversary this past weekend.

Special synagogue services included memorial prayers for Mrs. Vickie Freedman, recently deceased president of the synagogue Women's Auxiliary. Also held was installation of officers. Installed were: President, Joseph Gibely II; vice president, Isaac Hasday; secretary, Victor Havian, and treasurer, Jack Yonis.

A dinner-dance was held Sunday to culminate the weekend festivities.

Congregants of the Tifereth Israel Synagogue are descended from Spanish (Sephardic) Jews who lived in that country prior to the fall of Jerusalem in 70 B.C. There they flourished and numbered among them physicians, bankers, skilled artisans and the greatest of Jewish scholars. The Spanish Inquisition (about the time of the discovery of America) saw the Jews dispersed throughout western Europe and Palestine.

The ancestors of the Peabody Congregation traveled to Turkey, where they took their places among the workers of that community.

The lure of America gripped the Sephardic Jew of Turkey and in 1911 the first of their number, Leon Eskenas and Myer Benater arrived in this area where they were soon joined by their wives Rebecca Eskenas and Regine Benater.

Shortly thereafter, the Gibely, Eskenazi, Yonis, Hasday, Leon, Havian, Pernitchi, Savy, Fermon and Erera families arrived and from this small group the sephardic synagogue, Congregation Tifereth Israel of Peabody and Salem emerged. (This synagogue is the only sephardic congregation north of Rhode Island.)

The Sephardic Jews have retained many of the customs acquired during the years their ancestors spent in Spain and the congregants speak a fluent “Ladino” (Spanish) despite the fact that not one of their number has set foot on the Spanish mainland in almost 5 centuries.

Tifereth Israel has never numbered more than 35 adult male members, although this number has remained constant and active in the 50 years since the congregation's inception. With the exception of the Leon, Erera and Menater families, whose descendants have moved out of the Salem-Peabody area, the children and grand-children of the congregation founders still remain active members of the synagogue.

Of the original group who arrived here in 1911, only Rebecca Eskenas is alive today. She is living in retirement in Florida.

items.title: After centuries of persecution, Peabody is home for Sephardic Jews
items.caption: Joseph Gibely in the sanctuary of Congregation Tifereth Israel.
items.description: The Peabody Times feature on Sephardic families' migration from Turkey and the history of Congregation Tifereth Israel, preserved in the Wyner Family Jewish Heritage Center collection.
items.source: The Peabody Times
items.citation: The Peabody Times, October 4, 1976, p. 3; Wyner Family Jewish Heritage Center, Jewish Community of Peabody Records I-581, Box 1, Folder 15, image 033
items.transcript:
October 4, 1976

PEABODY — In 1911, after 500 years of exile in Turkey, a small band of Jewish families migrated to America and re-established their close-knit, small Sephardic (Spanish) Jewish community in the Peabody-Salem area.


Today, the clan centers its religious and social life around their Temple, Congregation Tifereth Israel, which was founded in February, 1922. Once strictly Orthodox, the congregation is now more liberal, using English in addition to Spanish and Hebrew in its services.


The small, white clapboard building on Pierpont Street has a small Star of David on the front door, unpretentious but aristocratic -- just like the Sephardics.


The Temple is the heart of the community: its president and leader, Joseph Gibely, is a descendant of the original immigrants who settled here 65 years ago.


During the week preceding the High Holy Days, Gibely spent every night preparing the shul (temple) for the worship services; writing down the names of participants who would read from the prayer books; changing religious cloths to the holiday white; and arranging prayer books for the 100 congregants and their families.


Since the Temple has a moderate number of families (30 men), much of the work has to be done by the officers of the Temple and Gibely, as usual, devoted dozens of hours to work.


Gibely beams with pride whenever mention is made of the Temple; it is the center of his life, and he frequently speaks about it to area groups -- Jewish and non-Jewish. He loves to discuss the origins of his Sephardic community.


“Surprisingly enough, not many Jews know the history of oppression that the Sephardics suffered,” he said. Gibely interrupted the High Holy Days preparations to discuss his community.


“At my talks, some of the most frequently asked questions are, ‘Who are the Sephardic Jews?’ ‘Where did they come from?’ I answer these questions by giving a brief history of the Inquisition, and life in medieval Spain; two things which played such a vital role in the Sephardic Jewish life,” said Gibely.


In 14th century Spain, Jews often were forcibly converted, killed or driven out of the country. Many converted to escape persecution and death.


The ‘New Christians,’ as they were officially called, could legally trade, enter universities, practice law, enter government and medical fields.


But the populace distrusted them, and called the converts ‘Marranos,’ a derisive term that meant ‘swine.’


“Outwardly, the Marranos were Christians; inwardly, they were Jews. Their disbelief in the dogmas of the church was notorious. They kept traditional Jewish ceremonies; some would eat only kosher meat; usually they married exclusively among themselves; they consorted with ex-coreligionists and sometimes furtively attended synagogue. Worst of all, in the eyes of the church, they transmitted their disbelief to their children,” explained Gibely.


The New Christians entered every profession -- even the church. In time, they all but dominated Spanish life; within a few generations, almost every aristocratic family had some Jewish blood in it.


They held fiercely to their Jewish faith. Without schools, without books, without leadership, and in constant danger of being discovered, they held on.


Finally, in 1464, the church began inquiring into the conduct of the New Christians, after some converts had been found celebrating Passover.


“Several prisons were given the power to investigate heretics. By 1481, the first converts were tried, judged guilty of heresy, and burned alive. During the next 350 years, the Spanish Inquisition tried 400,000 subjects; 30,000 were put to death,” said Gibely.


“It wasn’t until 1834 that the institution of the Inquisition was finally abolished.”


In the meantime, those who had remained open, practicing Jews, also suffered in Spain and Portugal.


They were barely tolerated and often attacked and murdered in those two countries during the Middle Ages. In 1492 the entire Jewish community was expelled from Spain, at the decree of Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand. In 1497, the Jews were also expelled from Portugal.


“It was at this point in history that thousands of Jewish immigrants fled into all parts of the Ottoman Empire (including North Africa and Asia Minor) and also to Italy,” said Gibely.


Other Spanish refugees established communities in Germany, Denmark, Holland, England, Austria and Hungary.


The ancestors of the Peabody Sephardics “probably left Spain in the late 1400’s and settled in Constantinople, Turkey, where they remained for the next 500 years,” said Gibely.


Then in 1911 the Peabody ancestors decided to emigrate to America, starting in 1911 came Leon and Rebecca Eskenas, Myer and Regina Benater; then the Gibely, Eskenazi, Yonis, Haday, Leon, Havian Pernitchi, Savy, Fermon and Erera families. They formed the nucleus of the present community known as the Congregation Tifereth Israel.


Gibely has been active in the Temple for 30 years, and president since 1972. He is the editor-in-chief of all the congregation’s newsletter; and master-of-ceremonies at all social events held at the temple for many occasions. He and wife, Victoria, have two sons, Morris, a teacher in Beverly, and Jack, an employe of JEC Tanning Co.


Associated with Fermon Tanning Corporation for 27 years, he is also the shop steward, officer of the employee welfare fund, member of the board of Local 21 Leather Workers for 10 years, and “unofficial interpreter for hundreds of Spanish-speaking residents.”


Gibely, like all of the members of the Sephardic congregation, speaks and reads Spanish, though the style is a little different from modern Spanish.


“The Sephardic Jews took their language with them, and over the centuries, has continued to speak medieval Spanish. In Turkey, we added some Turkish expressions, so Ladino, our Spanish, is a strange blend of Spanish and Turkish.”


In all parts of the world, the Sephardics kept their Spanish idiom, as the language of speech and as a literary medium. In addition to Hebrew, Ladino is used at all services.


“Now, we use more English so everyone can understand the service,” said Gibely.


“When our parents lived in Turkey, they spoke five or six languages fluently because of the cosmopolitan makeup of the community.


“In America, though, the second congregation doesn’t speak quite as many languages.


Last July 26, Gibely was presented a plaque “acknowledging with great pride his many contributions and unselfish efforts on behalf of the congregation”; on it was also inscribed Gibely’s favorite expression, one which he invariably utters to everyone: “May you go from strength to strength.” This is Gibely’s philosophy, and, he feels, the philosophy which has enabled the Sephardics to survive through the hostile centuries.

October 4, 1976

PEABODY — In 1911, after 500 years of exile in Turkey, a small band of Jewish families migrated to America and re-established their close-knit, small Sephardic (Spanish) Jewish community in the Peabody-Salem area.

The Temple is the heart of the community: its president and leader, Joseph Gibely, is a descendant of the original immigrants who settled here 65 years ago.

During the week preceding the High Holy Days, Gibely spent every night preparing the shul (temple) for the worship services; writing down the names of participants who would read from the prayer books; changing religious cloths to the holiday white; and arranging prayer books for the 100 congregants and their families.

Since the Temple has a moderate number of families (30 men), much of the work has to be done by the officers of the Temple and Gibely, as usual, devoted dozens of hours to work.

PEABODY — Sunday, June 29, will be a big day at Congregation Tifereth Israel on Pierpont Street.

It will be what Joe Gibely II, congregation president, describes as “one of the most important and pleasurable milestones in the 64-year history of the synagogue.”

The Leo Gibely Study, presented by Rabbi Dov and Barbara Pikelny, will be dedicated and an open house, featuring the newly renovated function room on the first floor, will take place.

Everyone is excited about the day’s events and delighted that “Uncle Leo” is being honored.

For the past three decades, octogenarian Leo Gibely has acted as spiritual advisor to the congregation. As the synagogue’s patriarch, he sets the religious standards and rules for the congregation, chants a portion of the service in the Sephardic style and maintains the continuity of the community.

“Uncle Leo still conducts worship services with Rabbi and Barbara Pikelny and myself and it’s a pleasure to sit back and listen to him belt out tunes, Sephardic style, during the holidays. If you want to hear chanting like that, you’d have to visit Sephardic congregations in New York, Alabama, or Israel, and we look forward to it year after year. It’s more Turkish or Arabic sounding than what one expects from the conventional worship,” Joe Gibely said.

Without a doubt, Uncle Leo is the oldest member of the synagogue, which was established in February of 1922 by Jews from Constantinople, (now Istanbul) Turkey. The congregants are descendants of Jews who fled Spain during the Inquisition, 500 years ago. Their language, other than the religious language of Hebrew and the secular language of English, continues to be Ladino, which derives from the pure Castilian Spanish of their ancestors and includes a mixture of Greek, Turkish and now English.

“As a child, ‘Uncle Leo’ Gibely (as he is known to everyone) received private tutoring in the Talmud because his parents were determined that he would never forget his heritage. When he was in Constantinople, he worked on Persian rugs — sewing and cutting. After arriving in the United States in 1916, he attended night school to learn English and met another Sephardic Jew, Esther, whom he married in 1923. They had four children, Joseph, Victor, Aaron and Rose and celebrated their golden wedding anniversary in 1973. Esther died the following year.

Gibely worked in the leather industry until his retirement from A.C. Lawrence in 1965; and in 1978, at the age of 77, he had a triple by-pass and valve operation for a very painful heart condition, according to his nephew, Joe, who adds, “Uncle Leo’s number one love, besides his family, is his total dedication to his synagogue.”

Joe Gibely describes the congregation’s patriarch, as, “Truly and without fanfare, a man who best exemplifies that which is good in all of us and today, in this troubled world, more of his type would eradicate a good deal of the problems that beset us. He is God fearing, kind, sincere, honest, hard working, fair, understanding, amiable and above all, an outstanding American and a good Jew. Presentation of the study by Rabbi and Barbara couldn’t have a more deserving recipient.”

In addition to viewing the Leo Gibely Study, visitors will be able to view the other work recently completed at the synagogue. Two rooms, two closets and three alcoves have been transformed. The lavatories have been relocated; there is a new ceiling, new lights, new floor, new doors, a new and modern kitchen and new paneling.

“All this and more was necessary for the beautiful and larger function room now on the first floor,” said an excited Joe Gibely, who adds, “One has to see it to believe it. It was a cooperative charity, determination and planning by the members of the congregation that brought this about.”

October 31, 1992

April 14–20, 1995

By Judith S. Antonelli · Advocate Staff

This week we continue our weekly series, Our Towns, that reports on the pulse of Jewish communities throughout Massachusetts. We explore Jewish life within that community, talk to synagogue leaders and residents, and provide readers with a close-up view of each town in the Commonwealth. This week, Our Towns visits Peabody.

Peabody’s Jewish history dates back to the turn of the century, when both Ashkenazi and Sephardic immigrants chose the thriving leather-manufacturing town as their new home.

By the 1930s, Peabody had 350 Jewish families, and by the mid-1960s, 1,700 Jewish families lived there. Today there is little movement into Peabody, but the population has remained stable. The current president of the city council is a Jewish woman.

Peabody is a major focal point of Jewish activity on the North Shore. It has a kosher butcher and bakery, and is the home of the Holocaust Center of the North Shore, directed by Sonia Weitz and Harriet Wacks.

Peabody also has its own Jewish Community Center, which split off from the JCC in Marblehead and became independent last September. The Peabody center serves 250 families in 22 communities with a day care center and a variety of programs for all ages. The JCC currently rents a building, but its long-range plans are to build a new center—perhaps on the grounds of Temple Ner Tamid, Peabody’s Conservative synagogue, says JCC President Debbie Poin.

Peabody’s oldest synagogue, Congregation Sons of Israel, was founded in 1909 by six families from Russia, Poland, and Lithuania. Another synagogue, Anshe Sfard, also came out of that original group, but it closed in the 1970s; its ark, memorial tablets, and remaining members became part of Congregation Sons of Israel.

Sons of Israel was Orthodox until 1962, when it modified its services with some English and instituted mixed seating. It now has 140 members, mostly elderly. By choice, the synagogue has no rabbi.

“We have a family spirit and are very close-knit,” said M. Irving Herbstner, ritual director. “We give kavod [honor] to everybody.”

A family service is held one Friday night a month. Adult education focuses on reading Hebrew and studying the prayers. Sons of Israel also serves as the headquarters of the Jewish War Veterans Post No. 220.

Around the same time that the Ashkenazi immigrants were starting Sons of Israel, a group of Sephardic Jews came to the area from Turkey. Settling first in the Castle Hill section of Salem, they moved to Peabody and formed Congregation Tifereth Israel in 1922, acquiring their own building in 1954.

Tifereth Israel, one of the oldest Sephardic congregations in New England, has 50 families. Its activities include holiday and anniversary celebrations, and meldathot—the Sephardic term for yahrzeit.

“We have a deep and proud tradition that existed prior to the Inquisition in Spain,” says President Joseph Gibely II. “We would never submit to Catholicism, so we went to Turkey. The Ottoman Empire was very tolerant. We got along with everyone and it was not unusual [for someone] to be able to speak four or five languages.”

“Our women picked up the cooking habits of all these groups,” he added, describing such delicacies as stuffed grape leaves, lamb with eggplant or string beans, stuffed tomatoes, and spinach pie.

As a youngster in Peabody, Gibely recalls, there was a great deal of discrimination by Ashkenazi Jews. A shopkeeper once referred to the Gibely family as “Gypsy Jews,” and another told him that Sephardic customs—such as naming a child after a living relative—were “wrong” and “not Jewish.”

“With maturity and evolution, that has changed,” Gibely declared. “There is enough trouble in this world without Jews fighting among themselves.” Tifereth Israel’s membership is open to Ashkenazi Jews (who adopt Sephardic prayer and pronunciation), the children are sent to Ashkenazi Hebrew schools, and the rabbi himself is Ashkenazi.

“A Jew is a Jew,” says Rabbi Dov Pikelny, who joined Tifereth Israel as a member after retiring from the rabbinate in 1980. “I chose to belong to this synagogue because it was peaceful, friendly, and had a good reputation. I thought I could serve them as an active member, but they asked me to be the rabbi. I agreed because it is such a wonderful group of people.”

In 1960 both a Conservative synagogue, Temple Ner Tamid, and a Reform synagogue, Temple Beth Shalom, were founded. Ner Tamid has 400 members and 150 students in its Hebrew school. Beth Shalom has 350 members and 240 students in its school.

“An interest in youth is what brought me into the rabbinate,” says Rabbi Abraham Morhaim, Ner Tamid’s rabbi for 29 years. As a result, the temple has three basketball teams and two volleyball teams and has won awards for its United Synagogue Youth programs.

Morhaim gave up his summer vacation 12 years in a row to take 65 teenagers to Israel for six weeks. Two other years he took them on a bus tour from New York to California, visiting Jewish communities and American historical sites.

“Teens are a very exciting group,” says Morhaim, who has been to Israel 35 times in 22 years. “They are energetic, bright, intelligent. If you learn how to reach them they can move mountains.”

Morhaim is retiring this year, but will continue in his other roles as instructor at the Gerim Institute (Conservative) and as chaplain of Children’s Hospital and the VA Hospital in Boston. He hopes to spend two or three months a year in Jerusalem.

Temple Beth Shalom’s specialty, according to Rabbi Philip Aronson, is providing “a meaningful liberal interpretation of Judaism for the North Shore... We have a warm and welcoming attitude towards intermarried families. The non-Jewish spouse is a member by marriage, and their backgrounds enrich us quite a bit.” Children raised as Jews are accepted as Jewish regardless of which parent is Jewish.

“Peabody has the largest concentration of unaffiliated Jews on the North Shore,” Aronson added. “We suspect a number of them may be intermarried, and we open our doors to them.”

Another unique program of Beth Shalom is the Chai Club, a “very lively group” of people who have been temple members for at least 18 years. “A number of them are founding members,” said Aronson, noting that the temple has a number of three-generation families as members.

items.transcriptHtml:
April 14–20, 1995

By Judith S. Antonelli · Advocate Staff

This week we continue our weekly series, Our Towns, that reports on the pulse of Jewish communities throughout Massachusetts. We explore Jewish life within that community, talk to synagogue leaders and residents, and provide readers with a close-up view of each town in the Commonwealth. This week, Our Towns visits Peabody.

Peabody’s Jewish history dates back to the turn of the century, when both Ashkenazi and Sephardic immigrants chose the thriving leather-manufacturing town as their new home.

By the 1930s, Peabody had 350 Jewish families, and by the mid-1960s, 1,700 Jewish families lived there. Today there is little movement into Peabody, but the population has remained stable. The current president of the city council is a Jewish woman.

Peabody is a major focal point of Jewish activity on the North Shore. It has a kosher butcher and bakery, and is the home of the Holocaust Center of the North Shore, directed by Sonia Weitz and Harriet Wacks.

Peabody also has its own Jewish Community Center, which split off from the JCC in Marblehead and became independent last September. The Peabody center serves 250 families in 22 communities with a day care center and a variety of programs for all ages. The JCC currently rents a building, but its long-range plans are to build a new center—perhaps on the grounds of Temple Ner Tamid, Peabody’s Conservative synagogue, says JCC President Debbie Poin.

Peabody’s oldest synagogue, Congregation Sons of Israel, was founded in 1909 by six families from Russia, Poland, and Lithuania. Another synagogue, Anshe Sfard, also came out of that original group, but it closed in the 1970s; its ark, memorial tablets, and remaining members became part of Congregation Sons of Israel.

Sons of Israel was Orthodox until 1962, when it modified its services with some English and instituted mixed seating. It now has 140 members, mostly elderly. By choice, the synagogue has no rabbi.

“We have a family spirit and are very close-knit,” said M. Irving Herbstner, ritual director. “We give kavod [honor] to everybody.”

A family service is held one Friday night a month. Adult education focuses on reading Hebrew and studying the prayers. Sons of Israel also serves as the headquarters of the Jewish War Veterans Post No. 220.

Around the same time that the Ashkenazi immigrants were starting Sons of Israel, a group of Sephardic Jews came to the area from Turkey. Settling first in the Castle Hill section of Salem, they moved to Peabody and formed Congregation Tifereth Israel in 1922, acquiring their own building in 1954.

Tifereth Israel, one of the oldest Sephardic congregations in New England, has 50 families. Its activities include holiday and anniversary celebrations, and meldathot—the Sephardic term for yahrzeit.

“We have a deep and proud tradition that existed prior to the Inquisition in Spain,” says President Joseph Gibely II. “We would never submit to Catholicism, so we went to Turkey. The Ottoman Empire was very tolerant. We got along with everyone and it was not unusual [for someone] to be able to speak four or five languages.”

“Our women picked up the cooking habits of all these groups,” he added, describing such delicacies as stuffed grape leaves, lamb with eggplant or string beans, stuffed tomatoes, and spinach pie.

As a youngster in Peabody, Gibely recalls, there was a great deal of discrimination by Ashkenazi Jews. A shopkeeper once referred to the Gibely family as “Gypsy Jews,” and another told him that Sephardic customs—such as naming a child after a living relative—were “wrong” and “not Jewish.”

“With maturity and evolution, that has changed,” Gibely declared. “There is enough trouble in this world without Jews fighting among themselves.” Tifereth Israel’s membership is open to Ashkenazi Jews (who adopt Sephardic prayer and pronunciation), the children are sent to Ashkenazi Hebrew schools, and the rabbi himself is Ashkenazi.

“A Jew is a Jew,” says Rabbi Dov Pikelny, who joined Tifereth Israel as a member after retiring from the rabbinate in 1980. “I chose to belong to this synagogue because it was peaceful, friendly, and had a good reputation. I thought I could serve them as an active member, but they asked me to be the rabbi. I agreed because it is such a wonderful group of people.”

In 1960 both a Conservative synagogue, Temple Ner Tamid, and a Reform synagogue, Temple Beth Shalom, were founded. Ner Tamid has 400 members and 150 students in its Hebrew school. Beth Shalom has 350 members and 240 students in its school.

“An interest in youth is what brought me into the rabbinate,” says Rabbi Abraham Morhaim, Ner Tamid’s rabbi for 29 years. As a result, the temple has three basketball teams and two volleyball teams and has won awards for its United Synagogue Youth programs.

Morhaim gave up his summer vacation 12 years in a row to take 65 teenagers to Israel for six weeks. Two other years he took them on a bus tour from New York to California, visiting Jewish communities and American historical sites.

“Teens are a very exciting group,” says Morhaim, who has been to Israel 35 times in 22 years. “They are energetic, bright, intelligent. If you learn how to reach them they can move mountains.”

Morhaim is retiring this year, but will continue in his other roles as instructor at the Gerim Institute (Conservative) and as chaplain of Children’s Hospital and the VA Hospital in Boston. He hopes to spend two or three months a year in Jerusalem.

Temple Beth Shalom’s specialty, according to Rabbi Philip Aronson, is providing “a meaningful liberal interpretation of Judaism for the North Shore... We have a warm and welcoming attitude towards intermarried families. The non-Jewish spouse is a member by marriage, and their backgrounds enrich us quite a bit.” Children raised as Jews are accepted as Jewish regardless of which parent is Jewish.

“Peabody has the largest concentration of unaffiliated Jews on the North Shore,” Aronson added. “We suspect a number of them may be intermarried, and we open our doors to them.”

Another unique program of Beth Shalom is the Chai Club, a “very lively group” of people who have been temple members for at least 18 years. “A number of them are founding members,” said Aronson, noting that the temple has a number of three-generation families as members.

items.description: Gary Band's Jewish Journal history of Congregation Tifereth Israel and its migration story from Constantinople to Peabody, published January 19, 2001.
items.source: The Jewish Journal

items.transcript:
January 19, 2001

Gary Band · Jewish Journal Staff

Joseph Gibely II of Peabody embodies the past, present and future of the North Shore’s only European Sephardic synagogue, Congregation Tifereth Israel on Pierpont Street in Peabody. For the past 28 years, Gibely has served as president of this intimate and welcoming congregation which was incorporated February 15, 1922. Though the shul claims only a 40-family membership, its rich history, empowering rabbi, and long tradition of lay leadership, may well propel Tifereth Israel through another 80 years of existence.

Gibely, 80, fluent in Spanish and Ladino, a language spoken by Sephardic Jews in Turkey, the Balkans, north Africa and the Americas, has the energy and appearance of a man 20 years his junior. Calling the temple his “number one love” after his wife of 58 years, Gibely sees to his myriad responsibilities with pride and dedication, carrying on traditions begun nearly four score ago. His late father, Morris, along with his uncles, one of whom became the first Jewish policeman in Salem, emigrated from Turkey in 1911.

They worked at Fermon Tanning in Peabody and, after a year of extremely difficult work, earned enough to send for their families back in Turkey. Joseph’s late mother Sarah, sister Stella and other family members came over in 1912 on the passenger ship Carpathia, famous for rescuing passengers from the sunken Titanic as they waited in life boats or clung to pieces of debris in the frigid north Atlantic.

When all members of Gibely’s immediate and extended multi-lingual family resettled on the North Shore, they began conducting services in each other’s homes in the Castle Hill section of Salem. The Congregation was led by Gibely’s late uncle Leo for 30 years and the cantor was the late Joseph Havian, “whose voice and delivery thrilled all of us with his beautiful Sephardic-style selections.” They were then renting space in back of an Ashkenazi shul called Knesset Y’Israel Anshen S’fard in Peabody, which later merged with Congregation Sons of Israel. Afterwards, they worshipped on the second floor of a building on Boston Street before obtaining their present-day location.

According to Gibely, the structure which became Tifereth Israel, built in 1906, was once owned by the Church of the Nazarene from whom it was purchased by the Congregation in 1957. The now roomy open spaces which comprise the temple’s social hall and sanctuary were once cubicles designed for private lessons and individual study. “If you saw the interior when it was first purchased, you wouldn’t believe it was the same place,” Gibely said, looking around the sanctuary as if for the first time.

Though they didn’t have much money, the first Tifereth Israel congregants did have something very important. The early congregation, according to Gibely, had in its possession three Sepher Torahs that have remained in the arc to the present day. “Not even with all the combined salaries of the first members could they have afforded one, let alone three Torahs,” he said. “How they got them I have no idea.”

When they purchased the building, each man assessed himself at $100. They each paid $5 per week into a yukes, a sort of communal bank. “The courage and determination of a small Sephardic congregation to have a place they could call their own was incredible,” said Gibely. “But initially, to leave their homeland, to lift up roots and start a new life here, took more courage than anything.”

Tifereth Israel has indeed changed dramatically over the years, evolving both esthetically and spiritually, thanks to numerous contributions from congregants past and present. According to Gibely, although some families have moved on, others whose parents and grandparents were once members always come back for the High Holidays.

“They come from Framingham, New Hampshire, out of respect.” He is especially thankful for the role played by their part-time spiritual leader, “retired” Rabbi Emeritus Dov Pikelny of Marblehead who was invited to assist the congregation in 1981. He and his late wife Barbara were like angels. She was a wonderful cantress who reorganized our choir, and the rabbi has been just wonderful. He has given us things we can’t measure: a pride in Judaism, a love of learning and the chance to emulate our ancestors. We’re very thankful for him.”

Rabbi Pikelny, though not Sephardic himself, feels blessed to have been given the opportunity to work with the “wonderful people” who make up the congregation. Although he leads them during the High Holy days, the Congregation’s monthly Shabbat service is led by Gibely and the songs and prayers beautifully chanted by Cantress Joanne Pressman. Her husband Jerry is descended from Joseph Pernitchi, one of the original seven charter members. Gibely is also thankful for people like Thomas Bloom of Danvers who sounds the shofar on the High Holidays and Benjamin Bejar of Boston who reads from the Torah.

Sheryl Becker of Danvers, a warm and engaging Sephardic woman, and the youngest member of the Congregation, makes up in voice and spirit what the congregation lacks in number. Becker, 33, studied and became a bat mitzvah under Rabbi Pikelny over 20 years ago at Temple Shalom in Salem. Four years ago, she was involved in a car accident caused by a woman driving the wrong way on an exit ramp off Route 128. Her seven-month recovery required that she practically relearn everything she ever knew, including her name, how to walk, speak and read both English and Hebrew. Becker, who shortly after her recovery began attending services on a regular basis, exemplifies a love for and commitment to Tifereth Israel.

“I would go to synagogue and remember parts of some of the songs,” she said. “Then by singing them over and over, I learned how to read the Hebrew again. I never thought I’d be able to do this. It’s almost like being re-bat mitzvahed.”

Everyone was really supportive. They would ask me how I feel, and I could only raise my arms and say ‘I’m just happy to be.’ As the person in charge of calling everyone to come to services, she worries about the future of the congregation. “If I wasn’t here who knows if people would come to services or if the synagogue will go on. It bothers me. But I know I survived for a reason.”

Whether or not Tifereth Israel continues will depend largely on the commitment of the congregants to sustain the core membership, and increase the size of the congregation through outreach and programming. But as Gibely says, “The size of a congregation doesn’t matter. In Israel there’s a temple on every corner. Some have 15 members, some have 50. The important thing is to keep the continuity and tradition going. I believe Tifereth Israel will continue for a long time because we have a young nucleus of people, an active group of members, and a terrific Ladies Auxiliary.”

Tifereth Israel, 8 Pierpont Street in Peabody, conducts monthly services and welcomes the community to worship with them. For more information, contact the temple at 978-531-8135.

One of the original seven charter members of Tifereth Israel, Morris Gibely (c) pictured in 1914 with his wife Sarah, brother David and children Rose, Robert and Stella. Their youngest child, Joseph, the Congregation’s president for the last 28 years, was born six years later.

AMY SESSLER POWELL
Jewish Journal Staff

PEABODY — Victoria Linsky remembers the joy her mother felt walking into Congregation Tifereth Israel, a Sephardic shul celebrating its 90th anniversary this year.

“Whenever my mother walked into the synagogue, her hands went up and kissed the Torah from afar, like a blessing in her heart. I do the same as my mother and I think of her,” said Linsky, 88, of [text incomplete in supplied transcription].

The only Sephardic synagogue north of Boston, Tifereth Israel has been in continuous operation since February of 1922. Many of the descendants of the founding family are still active there.

In the 90-year history, there have been just seven presidents and two rabbis — Dov Pikelny from 1982 to 2001, and Howard Kosovske from 2008 until now. During the rest of the time, “leadership and prayers were led by people in the congregation, mostly related to original founders. We have a real tradition and heritage,” Joanne Pressman, granddaughter of founders Joseph Havian and Joseph Pernitchi, and soloist and co-officiant in services since 1991.

Congregation Tifereth Israel is one of three older synagogues in the area celebrating important milestones. The Walnut Street Shul in Chelsea turns 125 this year, and Winthrop's Temple Tifereth Israel kicked off a centennial last month.

Any synagogue that survives that long generally finds itself dealing with some challenges. For example, the Walnut Street Shul hails from a time when there were more than 16 shuls in Chelsea. Today, with seating for 1,180 people, they struggle to form a minyan on Shabbat, though they generally have better luck during the week, said Herb Kupersmith of Marblehead, who vowed to his late mother to keep the shul open.

Many come to Walnut Street to photograph the beautiful arched and painted ceiling and the 38.5-foot oak ark.

“The shul has a glorious past. I was bar mitzvahed there,” Kupersmith said, acknowledging that he knows of no Jewish children in the Chelsea public schools today. Still, he expects 250 people to show up for the celebratory breakfast on October 14. Many people across the North Shore retain deep loyalty to the shuls of their childhood.

Winthrop's Tifereth Israel is struggling with the size of the building, but recently struck an agreement with the Chelsea Jewish Foundation and will soon be working together on a project that will bring over-55 housing and a smaller synagogue to its property. The new building will be more size appropriate and energy efficient. Burt Figler said, “We are all sort of anxious for the new place.” The Winthrop synagogue is the only one in its area with a religious school, currently with 14 students, but that has helped them attract some young families, Figler said. They hope to grow the program in the coming years, he added.

The lack of a religious school has challenged Peabody's Tifereth Israel. President Elliot Hershoff said members in need of a religious school often join a second synagogue. Now, with a rabbi, they have more programs and hope to attract younger members who will keep things going when the older generation can no longer do so.

Fran Arsenault-Shaheen said that over the years, whenever they have worried about someone taking over a job, a person usually steps forward. She, too, is a member of the founding families, but sees that the younger generations are more spread out geographically or not interested in taking over. Growing up, Arsenault-Shaheen and her cousins, Pressman and Millie Becker, recall the joy of going to a synagogue where nearly everyone was related.

“We were not quite a family shul because we always branched out to others, but it is very important to me and has been all my life,” she said.

Arsenault-Shaheen described the way family members took care of everything around the shul.

“My father (Isaac Hasday) was like a custodian to the synagogue. Whenever anything needed to be done, he and Joanne Pressman's/Millie Becker's mother (my Aunt Sophie Pernitchi) along with a cousin, Lionel Harsfield, and a few others took on the task. My father was on the board of directors and was vice-president until he died in 1999. My mother (Rose Hasday) was very involved in ladies auxiliary as well as the synagogue. My mother and Joanne and Millie's mother (Sophie) sewed all the chair covers for the sanctuary of our current synagogue when we first moved in,” Arsenault-Shaheen said.

Becker said the synagogue has a tradition that when a family member is called to the Torah, the other family members stand. Many years ago, if anyone in her family was called, it seemed like the whole crowd stood. During this last round of High Holy Days, she saw a big change.

“Now there are just three or four of us,” she said, but she saw [continuation not supplied].

items.transcript:
November 1, 2018

On October 18, 2018, the Jewish Journal published an article by Michael Wittner titled “Jewish Peabody: Pride and Perseverance.” I was dismayed to read that there were only three synagogues in Peabody, when there are four. Our synagogue, Congregation Tifereth Israel, is a small but active congregation on Pierpont Street in Peabody.

Our synagogue is 96 years old and has been at the same location for over 60 years. We are a small but active community. We hold services every Friday night and Saturday morning, as well as all the holidays. We have an active Sisterhood and Men’s Club, and have several social events throughout the year.

We are currently without a rabbi, and are searching for one. Our congregation is made up of Jews from all backgrounds, including Sephardic and Ashkenazi. We are a welcoming congregation, and invite anyone who is interested to attend our services and events.

I hope this letter sheds some light on who we are.

Elliot Hershoff
President
Congregation Tifereth Israel
Peabody

August 29, 2019

PEABODY – Next month, if you happen to pass by Congregation Tifereth Israel in Peabody, someone might call out, “Para muchos años!”

That is the equivalent of “L’Shana Tova” in Ladino, a mixture of Spanish and Hebrew spoken by Sephardic Jews. Ladino blessings are still recited after many prayers at Tifereth Israel, the only Sephardic congregation on the North Shore. Though intermarriage with the larger Ashkenazi community has changed the original makeup of the congregation, it retains a Sephardic identity.

“On a Friday night when we light the candles, I say the original Hebrew blessing, but then I follow it up with a Ladino blessing,” said Joanne Pressman, the cantorial soloist who is also descended from two of the original founders. “The Sephardic prayer book has a lot of extra words – if people come and are singing along and not looking at the book, they’re like, ‘Wow, the Kaddish is much longer’… There’s other prayers that even though you recognize the prayer and the melody, all of a sudden, the words change.”

Tifereth Israel still observes uniquely Sephardic customs. “We have a Sephardic tradition where when someone is called for an Aliyah to the Torah, those who are related to them stand up as a sign of respect for them,” said Pressman. “There would be times when half the congregation would stand.”

The Tifereth Israel of Pressman’s youth was a tight-knit congregation of Turkish Jews, many of whom had immigrated to Peabody to work in the city’s leather industry and avoid conscription in the Ottoman military. It was founded on Feb. 15, 1922 by seven Turkish immigrants, including both of Pressman’s grandfathers, Joseph Pernitchi and Joseph Havian. In the early years, the congregation had no permanent building, and services were conducted in private homes.

Congregation Tifereth Israel was founded in 1922.

“They were like wanderers – they didn’t have their own shul, so they went to different places, and used their facilities,” said the temple’s president and spiritual leader, Elliot Hershoff, who is both the longest-serving and the first Ashkenazi president. “Many years ago when they came to this country, they bought a piece of land, and were going to build a synagogue there, but that never came to fruition.”

In 1955, the congregation purchased a house on Pierpont Street, where it continues to this day.

Doris Hershoff, who is Elliot’s wife and has attended the congregation her entire life, said that she felt excluded from the Peabody’s Ashkenazi Jewish community in her youth. “I did feel separate, like they didn’t understand us,” said Doris, who grew up in a Sephardic Turkish family, but married an Ashkenazi man. “I always tell the story of when Elliot took me to meet his mother, and she thought I wasn’t Jewish, and she told Elliot he couldn’t marry me. He said, ‘Mom, she’s more religious than we are!’”

items.description: Adam Bass's February 10, 2022 Weekly News article about CTI's centennial and planned June anniversary dinner.
items.source: Weekly News

items.transcript:
February 10, 2022

Congregation Tifereth Israel, a Sephardic synagogue, is turning 100 years old on Feb. 15.

To celebrate the occasion, the temple will be holding an anniversary dinner at the Continental Restaurant on Jun. 12, 2022. More details about the dinner will be released in their newsletter.

Congregation Tifereth Israel was founded on Feb. 15, 1922 by several Sephardic Jewish families who had immigrated to Peabody and Salem primarily from the country of Turkey.

Sephardic Jews, or Sephardim, are members of the Jewish Diaspora whose ancestors settled in the Iberian Peninsula, known today as Spain and Portugal. The term Sephardim comes from the Hebrew word Sefarad, or Spain.

Sephardic Jews also lived in Turkey and Greece and, in the early 1910s, some immigrated to the United States because of the uprisings, revolutions and wars in Turkey.

According to the Jewish Heritage Center of the North Shore, located in Lynn, one of the cities Sephardic Jewish immigrants were attracted to was Peabody, namely because of the leather industry. Many Sephardic settlers were shoemakers by trade.

“The prosperity of the town was thus attributed to the leather businesses, which continued to grow,” the Heritage Center said. “The more factories, the more businesses.”

As for Congregation Tifereth Israel, many of those same immigrants who fled Turkey went on to found the synagogue. They were forced to live as Catholics in Spain but carried their traditions in secret with their families. The Congregation’s foundation came at a time when Sephardic Jews were not as comfortable with the newly-formed Ashkenazi synagogue. Ashkenazi Jews are those who descend from Eastern European countries such as Poland, Russia or Lithuania.

Sephardic services vary from Ashkenazi styles; for instance, Sephardic Jews may speak Ladino — a Judeo-Spanish language — as opposed to Yiddish, a Judeo-Germanic language spoken by many Ashkenazi families.

Despite their differences, Tifereth Israel is on very good terms with the Ashkenazi community in Peabody and welcomes them into their congregation, as they too are family. From humble beginnings to finding community in Peabody, this congregation has lasted for 100 years and seeks to keep moving forward year after year, generation after generation.
